column1: What harmonic content does a sawtooth wave contain, and how do amplitudes decay?
column2: All harmonics (odd and even), with amplitude decaying inversely with harmonic number (A_n ∝ 1/n), i.e. 6 dB/octave rolloff.

column1: What harmonic content does a square wave contain, and how do amplitudes decay?
column2: Only odd harmonics, with amplitude decaying as A_n ∝ 1/n for odd n (same 1/n rolloff as sawtooth, but only odd partials).

column1: What harmonic content does a triangle wave contain, and how do amplitudes decay?
column2: Only odd harmonics, with amplitude decaying as the inverse square of harmonic number (A_n ∝ 1/n²), i.e. 12 dB/octave rolloff — much steeper than the square wave.

column1: What does a sine wave contain in terms of harmonics?
column2: Only the fundamental frequency with zero harmonics, producing a pure, colorless tone.

column1: What mathematical theorem underlies the claim that any periodic waveform can be decomposed into sine waves at harmonic frequencies?
column2: Fourier series/Fourier analysis (Joseph Fourier, early 19th century).

column1: In subtractive synthesis, what is the architectural signal flow from sound source to output?
column2: Oscillator (harmonic-rich signal) → Filter (shapes spectrum) → Amplifier (shapes time-variant amplitude) → Output, with an Envelope Generator modulating both the filter cutoff and amplifier gain.

column1: What distinguishes a lowpass filter from a highpass filter in subtractive synthesis, timbrally?
column2: Lowpass preserves low frequencies and attenuates highs, creating warmth/darkness; highpass cuts bass/low-mids and passes treble, creating a thin, reedy, telephone-like tone.

column1: What does the resonance (Q) parameter do in a filter, and what physical mechanism produces it?
column2: Resonance creates a sharp amplitude peak at the cutoff frequency right before the attenuation slope; it is produced by positive feedback, where a portion of the filter's output is fed back into its input.

column1: What is the defining frequency range of an LFO versus an audio-rate oscillator?
column2: LFOs operate roughly 0.01–20 Hz (sub-audio, inaudible as pitch); audio-rate oscillators operate above ~20 Hz, perceived as pitch. Above ~10-20 Hz an LFO crosses into audio-rate territory and can generate audible modulation sidebands.

column1: What sonic effect results from routing an LFO to filter cutoff, to amplitude, and to pitch, respectively?
column2: Filter cutoff → wah effect; amplitude → tremolo; pitch → vibrato.

column1: What is the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem's constraint on digital synthesis at a 48 kHz sample rate, and what artifact occurs if violated?
column2: Only frequency content below 24 kHz (half the sample rate) can be faithfully reproduced; generating partials above this limit causes aliasing, which folds back as inharmonic distortion in the audible spectrum.

column1: What key architectural innovation did Wolfgang Palm's PPG Wave introduce, and what tradeoff did it represent?
column2: It stored single-cycle waveforms in ROM lookup tables (wavetables) instead of summing many sine oscillators for additive synthesis, trading CPU-bound harmonic computation for memory-bound table lookup (storage over computation).
